title: Antioxidant potency of gallic acid, methyl gallate and their combinations in sunflower oil triacylglycerols at high temperature.

Antioxidant potency of gallic acid, methyl gallate and their combinations in
sunﬂower oil triacylglycerols at high temperature
Reza Farhoosha,⁎, Laura Nyströmb
a Ferdowsi University of Mashhad, Faculty of Agriculture, Department of Food Science and Technology, P.O. Box 91775-1163, Mashhad, Iran
b ETH Zurich, Institute of Food, Nutrition and Health, Schmelzbergstrasse 9, 8092 Zurich, Switzerland
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Antioxidant
Hydroperoxides
Phenolic compounds
Polar components
Sunﬂower oil
A B S T R A C T
Lipid peroxidation and polar compounds formation in sunﬂower oil triacylglycerols at 120 °C were investigated
in the presence of gallic acid (GA), methyl gallate (MG), MG/GA combinations (75:25, 50:50, and 25:75), and
tert-butylhydroquinone (TBHQ). Hydroperoxide-based kinetic parameters (IP, induction period, min; ki, rate
constant during IP, meq/kg min) of control sample (38.0; 2.0346) were considerably improved by TBHQ (201.1;
0.0267), followed by GA (163.8; 0.0837), MG (151.2; 0.0983), and the combinations (∼184.4; ∼0.0861) with
an average synergy of 18.6%. Regarding the polar compounds inhibition, the best antioxidant performance (the
ratio of IP to oxidized triacylglycerol monomers at IP, min/%; time reaching 10% of triacylglycerol dimers and
polymers, min) in general belonged to MG/GA 75:25 (42.4; 263.0), GA (43.2; 249.9), MG (38.0; 237.5), and
TBHQ (17.7; 214.4), respectively. The kinetic parameters based on the formation of polar compounds than
hydroperoxides provided more reliable results to evaluate antioxidant potency at high temperature.
1. Introduction
Gallic acid (3,4,5-trihydroxybenzoic acid, GA) and its methyl ester
derivative, methyl gallate (MG), are among the prevalent phenolic
compounds
in
plant
kingdom
(Chanwitheesuk,
Teerawutgulrag,
Kilburn, & Rakariyatham, 2007; Rahman, Jeon, & Kim, 2016). They are
well known for a wide range of valuable biological eﬀects such as an-
tioxidant,
anti-inﬂammatory,
anti-apoptotic,
anti-microbial,
anti-
tumor, and anti-platelet activities, protection against DNA damage and
lung injury due to oxidative stress, and attenuation of diabetic oxidative
stress (Rahman et al., 2016; Rajan & Muraleedharan, 2017).
A limited number of studies conducted in recent years have shown
GA and MG to considerably prevent lipid oxidation under normal sto-
rage
conditions
(Asnaashari,
Farhoosh, & Sharif,
2014;
Farhoosh,
Johnny,
Asnaashari,
Molaahmadibahraseman, & Sharif,
2016;
Roidoung, Dolan, & Siddig, 2016). Additionally, a previous hydroper-
oxide-based evaluation of GA and MG indicated their impressive ability
to improve a number of thermal kinetic parameters of lipid oxidation
(Farhoosh,
Sharif,
Asnaashari,
Johnny, & Molaahmadibahraseman,
2016). Thermal treatments, which are frequently used to process food
materials, can drastically aﬀect the antioxidant eﬃciencies. Therefore,
antioxidants of high potency under such a harsh condition have always
been of special interest. tert-Butylhydroquinone [2-(1,1-dimethylethyl)-
1,4-benzenediol, TBHQ] is known to be one of the most powerful
synthetic antioxidants employed widely in food industry and also
considered to have really good resistance to thermal decomposition
and/or volatilization (Ying et al., 2010). Nevertheless, due to possible
toxic and carcinogenic eﬀects of synthetic antioxidants, TBHQ is not
allowed for food application in many countries (Pinho, Ferreira,
Oliveira, & Ferreira, 2000).
Lipid hydroperoxides, or primary oxidation products, are unstable
intermediates that easily decompose into a variety of secondary oxi-
dation products. The latter will not signiﬁcantly be produced unless the
concentration of hydroperoxides (meq/kg, called as peroxide value, PV)
reaches a critical point, PVIP (Fig. 1A), at the end of the initiation phase
of lipid peroxidation (Marquez-Ruiz, Martin-Polvillo, & Dobarganes,
2003). The time distance to this point is called induction period, IP,
which is the time before rapid deterioration in the propagation phase of
lipid peroxidation onwards. During IP, hydroperoxides slowly increase
with a rate constant ki (Fig. 1A) (Shim & Lee, 2011).
At high temperatures, a more complex group of oxidation products
of mainly higher polarity is produced. The analysis of polar compounds
is one of the most reliable methods of lipid oxidation monitoring under
thermally harsh conditions. Polar compounds are two sets of alteration
components formed through thermoxidative reactions and hydrolytic
cleavage of triacylglycerols. The ﬁrst set is comprised of oxidized

triacylglycerol polymers (TGP), and the second one consists of dia-

(DG)
and

acids
(FFA)
(Houhoula,
Oreopoulou, & Tzia, 2003) (Fig. 1B). The oxTGM, in turn, encompass a
wide range of oxidation products with one or more oxygenated func-
tional groups, such as peroxide group in lipid hydroperoxides, or epoxy,
keto, or hydroxyl groups in many of secondary oxidation products.
Hence, oxTGM measurement can be used to determine total oxidation,
which provides concomitant useful information on initial and advanced
stages of lipid oxidation. Dimeric, TGD, and polymeric, TGP, compo-
nents, which are very complex and structurally not fully identiﬁed, are
characteristic of advanced oxidation. Polymerisation compounds have
been shown to increase as the amount of oxTGM reduces during the
course of oxidation. In other words, more reactive molecules of oxTGM
are polymerised at high temperatures through oxygenated linkages
(Ruiz-Mendez, Marquez-Ruiz, & Dobarganes, 1997). A TGDP (TGD
+ TGP) content of 10% is a criterion that has received much attention
nowadays (Farhoosh & Tavassoli-Kafrani, 2011) because feeding trials

The aim of the present study was to evaluate the antioxidant po-
tency of GA and MG against the formation of lipid hydroperoxides and
diﬀerent polar components at a thermally harsh condition of 120 °C.
Moreover, the powerful synthetic antioxidant TBHQ, which could po-
tentially be replaced by these natural antioxidants, was used as a
standard for comparison in this study. To assess the antioxidant activ-
ities, sunﬂower oil, which is widely used with salads and as a frying oil,
and is considered to be a highly appreciated source of the essential
linoleic acid, was chosen as an oxidation environment.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
Commercial sunﬂower oil was purchased from the market and was
stored at −18 °C until use. All chemicals and solvents used in this study
were of analytical reagent grade and purchased from Sigma-Aldrich
(Buchs, Switzerland).
2.2. Sunﬂower oil puriﬁcation
The oil sample (150 g) was applied to a glass chromatographic
column (25 × 2.5 cm I.D.) packed with aluminium oxide 60 (100 g,
active, neutral), which had been activated at 200 °C for 3 h immediately
before use. The column and collection vessels were wrapped in alu-
minium foil, and the oil was drawn through the column by suction
without solvent (Yoshida, Kondo, & Kajimoto, 1992). The procedure
was repeated twice to reach insigniﬁcant amounts of lipid hydroper-
oxides and indigenous antioxidative compounds, such as tocopherols
and other phenolic compounds (see below).
2.3. Antioxidant treatments preparation
Puriﬁed sunﬂower oil samples (1.0 g) containing 0.6 µmol of the
antioxidants (TBHQ, MG, GA, and MG/GA 75:25, 50:50, and 25:75%w/
w) were prepared by adding aliquots of a solution of the antioxidant in
acetone to a weighed oil sample followed by the removal of the solvent
under nitrogen.
2.4. Oxidation monitoring
The antioxidant treatments were oxidized in a kinetic regime, i.e. at
a suﬃciently high oxygen concentration at which the diﬀusion rate
does not inﬂuence the oxidation rate (Emanuel, Denisov, & Maizuss,
1965). Glass containers (35.0 × 30.0 mm) containing a 1-mm layer of
the oil (∼650 mg) with no cap were stored in an oven at 120 °C. At
given time intervals, two containers from each antioxidant treatments
were taken and measured their primary (lipid hydroperoxides) and
secondary (polar components) oxidation products.
2.5. Analytical methods
Peroxide value, PV, as a measure of the content of lipid hydroper-
oxides was determined according to International IDF Standard method
74A:1991, as described by Shantha and Decker (1994). Total toco-
pherols content was determined according to the colorimetric method
described by Wong, Timms, and Goh (1988). The content of total
phenolics was determined spectrophotometrically using Folin–Cio-
calteau’s reagent according to the method described by Capannesi,
Palchetti, Mascini, and Parenti (2000). A calibration curve of gallic acid
in
methanol
was
performed
in
the
concentration
range
of
0.04–0.65 mg/ml.
Fatty acids were transesteriﬁed into their corresponding methyl
esters by vigorous shaking of a solution of oil in hexane (0.3 g in 7 ml)
with 2 mL of 7 N methanolic potassium hydroxide at 50 °C for 10 min.
The fatty acid composition was analysed by gas chromatography (HP-
5890 GC system, Hewlett-Packard, CA, USA) on CP-FIL 88 capillary
column of fused silica (60 m × 0.22 mm I.D., 0.20 µm ﬁlm, Supel Co.,
Inc., Bellefonte, PA) heated at 198 °C. The temperature of injector and
ﬂame ionization detector, FID, detector was maintained at 250 °C.
Nitrogen was the carrier gas with a ﬂow rate of 0.75 ml/min (Farhoosh,
Niazmand, Rezaei, & Sarabi, 2008).
Total polar compounds (TPC, %w/w) content was determined ac-
cording to the economical micro-method developed by Schulte (2004).
The altered compounds that constitute the polar fraction were sepa-
rated by high-performance size-exclusion chromatography (HPSEC),
according to Dobarganes, Perez-Camino, and Marquez-Ruiz (1988).
Isolated polar fractions were analysed in a Hewlett-Packard 1100 Series
HPLC system with a 20 µl sample loop. A refractive index, RI, detector
(PerkinElmer Inc.) and two Ultrastyragel columns (Waters Corp., Mil-
ford, MA, USA) with 100 Å (low MW ranged from 100 to 1000) and
500 Å (low MW ranged from 100 to 10,000) pore size connected in
series were operated at 40 °C. The columns were 300 × 7.8 mm I.D.,
packed with a macro-porous, highly cross-linked and spherical poly-
styrene/divinylbenzene copolymer (5 µm particle size). HPLC-grade
tetrahydrofuran, THF, served as the mobile phase with a ﬂow of 1 ml/
min. Sample concentration was 10 mg/ml in THF.
2.6. Kinetic parameters
2.6.1. Lipid hydroperoxides
Evolution of hydroperoxides during the oxidation at 120 °C led to
the kinetic curves consisted of two linear initiation and propagation
phases of lipid peroxidation (Fig. 1A). The x- and y-coordinates of the
intersection point of the two linear curves provided induction period,
IP, and PV at IP, PVIP, respectively (Farhoosh & Hoseini-Yazdi, 2013).
The kinetics before IP were regarded as pseudo zero-order reactions
(Shim & Lee, 2011). Eq. (1) is a function where the reaction rate does
not depend on the concentration of the oxidizing substrate. By in-
corporating the IP constants, Eq. (2) was derived.

2.7. Statistical analysis
All determinations were carried out in triplicate and data were
subjected to analysis of variance (ANOVA). ANOVA and regression
analyses were performed according to MStatC and CurveExpert
Professional 2.6.3 software. Signiﬁcant diﬀerences between means
were determined by Duncan’s multiple range tests; p values less than
0.05 were considered statistically signiﬁcant.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Sunﬂower oil characterization
The chemical characteristics of the unpuriﬁed and puriﬁed sun-
ﬂower oils are given in Table 1. The fatty acid composition, which was
not aﬀected by the chromatographic puriﬁcation, consisted mainly of
oleic and linoleic acids, in agreement with the amounts reported in
literature for sunﬂower oil (Grompone, 2005). The unpuriﬁed sun-
ﬂower oil had acceptable amounts of hydroperoxides and polar com-
pounds, as the PV and TPC of low oxidized and unused oils normally
range from 3.0 to 5.0 meq/kg (Warner, Frankel, & Mounts, 1989) and
from 0.4 to 6.4% (Lumley, 1988), respectively. The level of these initial
quality indicators was decreased to negligible amounts in the puriﬁed
oil. The oil sample examined in this study contained relatively con-
siderable contents of the indigenous antioxidative compounds (toco-
pherols and phenolic compounds), which were eﬃciently removed by
the puriﬁcation process.
3.2. Lipid hydroperoxide inhibition
Antioxidant potency can be evaluated by considering the length of
IP as well as the rate of lipid hydroperoxide formation during IP. Lipid
hydroperoxides, LOOH, are resulted from electrophilic attack of lipid
hydroperoxyl radicals, LOO%, as the predominant reactive radicals over
the course of lipid oxidation, to the other susceptible lipid substrates,
e.g. polyunsaturated fatty acids. Antioxidants inactivate LOO% by do-
nating hydrogen and produce LOOH plus stable antioxidant radicals
through the main reaction of chain termination (AH + LOO% →LOOH
+ A%). The antioxidants of higher eﬀectiveness are more eﬃciently
able to reduce LOO% and, therefore, prolong IP. However, the potential
participation of antioxidant molecules and/or their radicals in many
side reactions (chain initiation and/or propagation) leads to so-called
lower strengths, resulting in increased rate of LOOH formation during
IP (Yanishlieva & Marinova, 2003).
The oil sample depleted of naturally occurring antioxidants showed
an extremely high instability, so that its propagation phase of lipid
oxidation was rapidly attained (ki = 2.04 meq/kg min) in a very short
period of time (IP = ∼38 min) (Table 2). The natural phenolic com-
pounds considerably improved the kinetic parameters of primary oxi-
dation. During a statistically signiﬁcant longer IP, GA inhibited sun-
ﬂower oil oxidation with a rate constant, ki, signiﬁcantly lower than
that of MG. This was in contrast to the previous ﬁndings indicating a
much better activity for MG compared to GA when oxidizing bulk phase
oil systems at moderate thermal conditions (Asnaashari et al., 2014;
Kikuzaki, Hisamoto, Hirose, Akiyama, & Taniguchi, 2002). Methyl gal-
late has been shown to have a lower phenolic hydroxyl bond dis-
sociation enthalpy (OeH BDE, 70.9 kcal/mol vs. 71.5 kcal/mol) (Lu,
Nie, Belton, Tang, & Zhao, 2006) due to the methyl ester group of more
electron-donating (Torres de Pinedo, Penalver, & Morales, 2007) and
intramolecular
hydrogen-bonding
abilities
(Stockmann,
Schwarz, & Huynh-Ba, 2000). Moreover, a recent mechanistic study on
the antioxidant activity of some p-hydroxybenzoic acid derivatives in
ﬁsh oil at 35–55 °C showed that MG participates only in the main

reaction of chain termination. However, the activity of MG was not
considerably increased above 45 °C, although it still had a higher ac-
tivity compared to GA (Farhoosh, Sharif, & et al., 2016). This indicates
that high temperatures, especially the much higher one in the present
study (120 °C), probably cause MG molecules and/or its radical to
overcome an energy barrier and play some pro-oxidative role through
taking part in chain initiation and/or propagation reactions. On the
other hand, bulk phase oils have been considered as water-in-oil nano-
and/or micro-emulsions with lamellar structures and reverse micelles
that are stabilized by many amphiphilic compounds, such as FFA,
mono- and di-acylglycerols, phospholipids, sterols, and oxidation pro-
ducts, including hydroperoxides, alcohols, aldehydes, and ketones. The
interfaces formed between traces of water (0.02–0.05%) and oil are
recognized as the major sites of lipid oxidation reactions, where the
phenolic group of antioxidants are positioned and prevents the forma-
tion of reactive radicals (Budilarto & Kamal-Eldin, 2015). On this basis,
the antioxidants of higher polarity are expected to occupy larger spaces
of the water-oil interfaces and inhibit lipid peroxidation more eﬀec-
tively. Considering the partition coeﬃcient (log P) as a polarity index,
GA has been shown to be more polar than MG (−0.28 vs. −0.23)
(Asnaashari et al., 2014). This means that the water-oil interfaces
would have been occupied to a higher extent by GA than MG, due to
more markedly increased molecular mobilities paralleled to lowered oil
viscosity at 120 °C as well as the greater solubilisation of the more li-
pophilic MG molecules in the bulk phase oil (Laguerre et al., 2015).
The combinations of GA and MG caused longer IPs compared to
those calculated for each antioxidant alone, indicating a more powerful
inhibitory eﬀect on lipid peroxidation (Table 2). On average, a synergy
of 18.6% was observed at the ratios investigated. The signiﬁcantly
lower values of ki of the MG/GA combinations compared to MG alone
indicates the synergy contribution to the inhibition of chain initiation
and/or propagation reactions (Yanishlieva & Marinova, 2003) as well as
their possibly promoted incorporations into the interfacial regions of
association colloids (Budilarto & Kamal-Eldin, 2015). Nevertheless, the
higher contributions of more polar GA molecules in the combinations
provided no signiﬁcantly diﬀerent synergies. By introducing the self-
aggregation hypothesis, Laguerre et al. (2015) proposed the idea of
antioxidant capacity collapse due to the hydrophobic interactions in
aqueous systems. Similarly, hydrophilic antioxidants might create some
aggregates of lower tendency to move towards the water-oil interfaces
in bulk phase oils. The higher concentrations of GA molecules of ther-
mally increased mobility (Laguerre et al., 2015), which is likely to
enhance hydrogen-bonding forces in hydrophobic environments to
some extent (Farhoosh, Johnny, & et al., 2016), may lower the diﬀusion
of antioxidants to the actual site of oxidation reaction.
tert-Butylhydroquinone, TBHQ, exhibited the best antioxidant per-
formance against the sunﬂower oil peroxidation by remarkably im-
proving IP and lowering the rate of LOOH formation as well (Table 2).
Considering a ki value of less than one-third that of all other treatments,
TBHQ molecules seem to have participated more predominantly in the
main reaction of chain termination (Yanishlieva & Marinova, 2003).
Nevertheless, TBHQ has been shown to have an OeH BDE higher than
those of GA and propyl gallate (74.3 vs. 70.2 and 69.6 kcal/mol, re-
spectively)
(Guitard,
Paul,
Nardello-Rataj, & Aubry,
2016),
which
makes it relatively less eﬃcient in propagation reactions theoretically
(Hussain et al., 2003). Furthermore, TBHQ with a hydrophobic tertiary
butyl substituent has been considered to have a polarity much lower
(log P = 1.37) than those of MG and GA (Asnaashari et al., 2014),
denoting its lesser sharing in the water-oil interfaces (see Section 3.3).
Peroxide value at IP, PVIP, can be employed as a critical con-
centration of lipid hydroperoxides at the beginning of the propagation
phase of lipid oxidation, which literally associates with the critical
micelle concentration (CMC) when transitioning from the initiation to
propagation phase (Budilarto & Kamal-Eldin, 2015). At this point, the
micelles grown and oxidatively stabilized during the initiation phase
collapse and act as micro-reactors of the bimolecular reactions of
hydroperoxides (2LOOH →LOO% + LO% + H2O) at the propagation
phase. Regarding the PVIP as a threshold level of LOOH, after which
lipid peroxidation is excessively accelerated, lipid systems of higher
oxidative resistance are expected to possess lower PVIP, especially at-
tained at any longer induction times. The PVIP of the puriﬁed sunﬂower
oil was as high as 77.3 meq/kg which was reduced to less than 6.0 meq/
kg in the presence of TBHQ, followed by 13.5 meq/kg and statistically
the same concentrations of 15.4–16.2 meq/kg in the presence of GA and
the other treatments, respectively (Table 2).
3.3. Polar compounds inhibition
Unlike lipid hydroperoxides, which are merely considered to be
primary oxidation products, polar compounds represent a range of
primary and secondary oxidation products of undesirable direct impacts
on sensory and toxicological aspects of lipid systems (Marquez-
Ruiz & Dobarganes, 1996; Reindl & Stan, 1982). Therefore, antioxidant
performance can be evaluated most eﬃciently by analysing such a di-
verse group of oxidation products.
The harsh condition of puriﬁed sunﬂower oil oxidation provided no
signiﬁcant amount of the hydrolytic products (DG and FFA) in all an-
tioxidant treatments, indicating traces of water in bulk phase oils and
those resulting from the initiation reaction of hydroperoxides (LOOH
+ LH →LO% + L% + H2O) (Budilarto & Kamal-Eldin, 2015) were not
high enough to remarkably cause hydrolysis of triacylglycerols. How-
ever, as shown in Fig. 1B, the thermoxidative products, which were
predominantly comprised of oxTGM, exponentially rose over time. It
was interesting to ﬁnd that the thermoxidative polar components began
to signiﬁcantly increase before reaching IP. This was in contrast to the
ﬁndings of Martin-Polvillo, Marquez-Ruiz, and Dobarganes (2004) and
Marquez-Ruiz, Martin-Polvillo, Velasco, and Dobarganes (2008), who
showed sharp increase of oxTGM and signiﬁcant build up of TGD and
TGP at relatively low temperatures only when exceeding IP. Accord-
ingly, the kinetic regime of oxidation at 120 °C might have caused
higher contributions of non-peroxide oxTGM to be produced during the
initiation phase of the puriﬁed sunﬂower oil oxidation. This signiﬁes
that reliable oxidative evaluations, especially at high temperatures,
require additional measurements that are capable of monitoring hy-
droperoxide decomposition products.
Interestingly, the natural phenolic compounds and their combina-
tions were able to protect the puriﬁed sunﬂower oil signiﬁcantly more
than TBHQ (Fig. 2). In comparison with the results obtained from the
LOOH inhibition (Section 3.2), this shows more accordance with the
electron-based and interfacial phenomena governing the overall anti-
oxidant potency. In fact, lesser interfacial sharing of more hydrophobic
TBHQ of weaker electron-donating capacity is expected to provide
condition in which LOOH molecules are more drastically decomposed
into the other oxygenated products at 120 °C. This can cause the re-
duced concentrations of LOOH in the reaction environment and, as a
result, apparently more appropriate performance of TBHQ towards
primary oxidation.
Gallic acid acted more eﬃciently than MG in inhibiting monomeric
and polymeric polar components (Fig. 2). This was in line with its better
performance towards primary oxidation, resulting from the more ef-
fective interfacial activity at high temperature. A signiﬁcantly similar
eﬃciency and even higher regarding tTGDP10 was observed when in-
corporating a one-fourth contribution of GA into MG, but surprisingly,
the higher contributions exerted some antagonistic eﬀects. This can be
explained by partial removal of the antioxidants from the interface,
resulting from the probable formation of antioxidant aggregates in the
bulk phase oil (Laguerre et al., 2015), although this hypothesis needs
more analytical data to be conﬁrmed.
4. Conclusions
The present study demonstrated that high temperatures are likely to

steeply raise the formation of secondary oxidation products even prior
to the end of the initiation phase of lipid peroxidation. This clariﬁes
that drastic decomposition of lipid hydroperoxides at elevated tem-
peratures may cause the antioxidant evaluations solely based on mon-
itoring the primary oxidation products to provide quite misleading re-
sults. In addition, overall performance of antioxidants in bulk phase oils
depends concomitantly on their signiﬁcant part in free radical chain
reaction mechanism and surface activity. On these bases, the natural
phenolic compounds gallic acid and methyl gallate showed to be more
potent candidates than the powerful synthetic antioxidant TBHQ in
preventing total oxidation at high temperature. Moreover, despite the
weaker eﬃciency reported at low temperatures, gallic acid exerted
higher antioxidant activity at 120 °C, which indicated that overall an-
tioxidant performance is aﬀected remarkably by the molecular mobi-
lities as well as interfacial phenomena. Finally, a 75:25 ratio of methyl
gallate to gallic acid provided the best antioxidant potency, due prob-
ably to a more eﬀective balance of both antioxidants in the water-oil
interfaces.
